title: Finding faster quantum algorithms with agents and formal verification
gist: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI used independent teams of Gemini 4 agents, with every idea proof-checked in a new open-source Lean library, to cut quantum algorithm costs: 11.8x for an inertial confinement fusion circuit, 8x for a photochemical molecule, 2.5x for Cytochrome P450, 2.57x for a Grover's implementation and 290x for the arcsin routine. The authors concede the algorithms still exceed what first error-corrected quantum computers will offer, but pitch proof-checked AI search as a general accelerator of scientific discovery.

insights.claim: Even the best known quantum algorithms for important applications still require more resources than early error-corrected quantum hardware will be able to support, so algorithmic cost reduction is a gating factor for useful quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Algorithm-side efficiency gains pull forward the date quantum hardware becomes commercially useful; track resource-estimate reductions alongside qubit-count roadmaps.
insights.quote: some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support
insights.locator: Quantum computers could soon solve problems

insights.claim: Google DeepMind states that even after its agent-driven improvements, running these quantum algorithms in real scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Tempers near-term quantum advantage hype: the gains are significant but do not yet close the gap for chemistry or fusion workloads on first-generation machines.
insights.quote: Running these algorithms in scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide
insights.locator: Running these algorithms in scientific simulations

insights.claim: Resource-intensive quantum circuits cannot be tested on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, so their correctness must be proved mathematically rather than empirically.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Creates a structural need for formal-verification tooling in quantum software stacks — a niche where theorem-prover infrastructure becomes a moat.
insights.quote: we have to prove that they work mathematically
insights.locator: Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits

insights.claim: Google DeepMind used teams of Gemini 4 agents, each team working independently on a problem, with every proposed algorithmic improvement verified in the Lean theorem prover before entering a shared notebook.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern for AI-for-science: generative agents paired with a machine-checkable verifier, removing the hallucination risk that limits LLM use in high-stakes research.
insights.quote: These ideas were then verified with Lean, before entering a shared notebook.
insights.locator: Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams

insights.claim: In DeepMind's setup, agents from each independent team met every four hours at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas, and the computational cost of the circuits fell gradually as teams produced more effective ideas over time.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Suggests multi-agent collaboration structures (independent exploration plus periodic idea exchange) yield compounding results — relevant to agent-orchestration platform design.
insights.quote: Every four hours, agents from each team met at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas.
insights.locator: Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams

insights.claim: Google DeepMind built and is open-sourcing a new Lean library for quantum algorithms, along with problem specifications and verified solutions on GitHub, so collaborating agents' ideas carry mathematical correctness guarantees.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing the verification substrate positions Google as the standard-setter for AI-driven quantum algorithm research and lowers the barrier for competitors and academics alike.
insights.quote: we are open-sourcing our Lean library, problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub
insights.locator: In a new paper, we used teams of Gemini 4 agents

insights.claim: The authors argue that proof-checked AI search compresses work that once took years of manual design, shifting human researchers toward choosing problems and interpreting results, and that the approach could accelerate other areas of quantum computing and scientific discovery more broadly.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Signals the labor model of R&D shifting from manual design to problem-setting and supervision — a thesis for AI-for-science productivity across pharma, materials and energy.
insights.quote: Proof-checked AI search compresses work that once took years of manual design, empowering researchers to focus on choosing problems and interpreting results.

insights.claim: The authors attribute the results to the combination of human domain expertise in quantum algorithms and the way the agent teams were set up, with humans setting the research direction by specifying problems and supervising progress.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Domain expertise plus agent scaffolding, not raw model capability alone, drives the outcome — favors incumbents with deep in-house science teams.
insights.quote: Our knowledge of quantum algorithms, combined with the way we set up our agent teams, led to real scientific results.
insights.locator: We are also excited by the way

insights.claim: Gemini 4 agent teams cut the computing cost (a metric combining required qubits and operations) of a quantum circuit for calculating a property of inertial confinement fusion by 11.8x, and lowered required memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Fusion simulation is a flagship candidate quantum workload; a ~12x cost cut materially improves the feasibility timeline for quantum-assisted fusion design.
insights.quote: cut the required computing cost (a metric that combines required qubits and operations) by 11.8×, and lowered required memory from 5,650 to 4,338 error-corrected qubits
insights.locator: We found a quantum circuit that helps calculate

insights.claim: For Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most human medicines, the agent teams found a 2.5x improvement in quantum simulation cost and lowered memory from 481 to 333 qubits by replacing bulky memory lookups.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Drug-metabolism simulation is a key pharma use case for quantum; lower qubit requirements bring it closer to plausible early hardware.
insights.quote: they found a 2.5× improvement and lowered memory from 481 to 333 qubits, by replacing bulky memory lookups

insights.claim: For a common light-sensitive molecule involved in photochemical reactions, the agent teams made quantum simulation 8x cheaper by simplifying how the algorithm tracks particle positions and electric forces.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Photochemistry is hard for classical computers; cost cuts here widen the set of chemistry problems where quantum could beat classical.
insights.quote: the agent teams made quantum simulation 8× cheaper
insights.locator: The agents also reduced costs for simulating molecules

insights.claim: The agent teams found a 2.57x speedup for a specific implementation of Grover's algorithm, the foundational quantum search routine over unsorted lists.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: Improvements to foundational primitives propagate to every application built on them, compounding the value of the method beyond the headline use cases.
insights.quote: We found a 2.57x speedup for a specific implementation of Grover's algorithm
insights.locator: We also improved a fundamental quantum algorithm

insights.claim: The agent teams found a 290x speedup for arcsin, a common arithmetic routine used by many other quantum algorithms to load numbers into quantum states.
insights.speaker: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg and Ryan Babbush
insights.so_what: A two-order-of-magnitude gain in a widely reused building block suggests large untapped slack remains in quantum subroutines — overall resource estimates for many algorithms may fall further.
insights.quote: a 290x speedup for arcsin, a common routine that is used by many other quantum algorithms to load numbers into quantum states
insights.locator: We also improved a fundamental quantum algorithm
